question: Which objective lens requires the use of a special oil to prevent light from bending?
explanation: The 100x lens needs oil to bridge the gap between the glass and the lens because oil has the same light-bending properties as glass. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why is the iris diaphragm adjusted during slide examination?

options.A: To secure the glass slide tightly onto the platform
options.B: To clean dust off the glass objective lenses safely
options.C: To control the amount of light passing through the specimen
options.D: To move the mechanical stage left and right

explanation: Adjusting the diaphragm helps change how much light hits the sample, which makes fine details much easier to see against the bright background. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why must most bacterial specimens be stained before viewing under a standard light microscope?

options.A: Dyes make the glass microscope slides easier to clean afterward
options.B: Unstained bacteria are nearly transparent and lack contrast
options.C: Staining chemicals are required to kill dangerous live viruses
options.D: Bacteria naturally glow brightly under normal room light

explanation: Without color added by stains, microbes blend into the bright background light and cannot be seen clearly. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the main difference between a simple stain and a differential stain?

options.A: Simple stains require heating the slide, but differential stains do not
options.B: Simple stains use one dye, while differential stains use multiple dyes
options.C: Simple stains are used for viruses, while differential stains are for fungi
options.D: Differential stains only work on dead cells, unlike simple stains

explanation: A simple stain shows the shape of everything using one color, whereas a differential stain sorts bacteria into groups using a sequence of different reagents. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of heat-fixing a clinical smear?

options.A: To melt the glass slide so the bacteria sink inward
options.B: To speed up the drying process of a freshly collected liquid
options.C: To attach the specimen firmly to the slide and kill the cells
options.D: To bleach out unwanted background colors from the sample

explanation: Passing the slide through a flame coagulates cellular proteins, making the bacteria stick securely to the glass so they do not wash off during staining. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h3)

question: What happens if a clinical smear is prepared much too thick?

options.A: The staining dyes will dissolve completely without leaving any color
options.B: Heat fixation will automatically burn away all the excess organic matter
options.C: The slide will break immediately upon entering the microscope stage
options.D: Individual bacteria will be hidden because the layers overlap

explanation: A thick clump of cells blocks light and traps stains, preventing the viewer from seeing individual bacterial shapes and arrangements clearly. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h3)

question: What color do Gram-positive bacteria appear after completing the full Gram stain procedure?
explanation: Gram-positive cells have thick cell walls that trap the crystal violet dye during the decolorization step, making them look purple under the microscope. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h4)

question: A laboratory scientist forgets to add the decolorizer step during a Gram stain. What will most bacteria look like under the microscope?

options.A: All bacteria will appear pink or red
options.B: No bacteria will be visible on the slide at all
options.C: Only the Gram-negative bacteria will be visible

explanation: Without the alcohol wash to strip the crystal violet out of thin cell walls, all cells keep the initial purple stain regardless of their actual type. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h4)

question: Which component in the cell wall of mycobacteria makes them resist standard staining methods?
explanation: Mycolic acid creates a tough, waxy barrier that prevents ordinary water-based stains from entering the cell easily. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why is acid-alcohol used in the Ziehl-Neelsen staining procedure?

options.A: To kill all live bacteria before the slide is looked at
options.B: To wash the red stain out of non-acid-fast cells
options.C: To act as the primary dye that colors the bacterial wall
options.D: To fix the clinical sample firmly onto the glass slide

explanation: Acid-alcohol strips the red carbolfuchsin dye away from ordinary cells, while acid-fast bacteria hold onto the color because of their waxy walls. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h5)

question: How can a laboratory worker verify that a freshly prepared batch of staining reagents is working correctly?

options.A: By skipping the heat-fixation step during the trial run
options.B: By testing the stains using known control organisms
options.C: By smelling the liquid for signs of chemical breakdown
options.D: By boiling the reagents on a hot plate for five minutes

explanation: Running a slide with bacteria of known characteristics ensures the stains react properly before testing real patient samples. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard safety practice in a clinical microbiology laboratory?

options.A: Pipetting liquid clinical samples by mouth
options.C: Wearing protective gloves and lab coats
options.D: Wiping down work surfaces after staining

explanation: Mouth pipetting is extremely dangerous and strictly forbidden because it risks swallowing infectious biological fluids. [learn more](BMP116_U1_T3#BMP116_U1_T3_h6)
